impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to administering a genus of antibodies to treat headache requires the same breadth-of-genus analysis applied in Amgen v. Sanofi to composition claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, over a dissent arguing the panel's approach undermines Amgen v. Sanofi enablement standards for genus claims. The denial preserves the panel ruling that method claims covering a broad genus of antibodies can satisfy enablement even where identifying members of the genus is difficult, so long as any member of the genus would be effective for the claimed treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biological molecules benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, allowing them to maintain broader patent protection over biologic therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face stronger barriers to invalidating broad biologic method claims on enablement grounds, potentially delaying biosimilar and competing product entry.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in patents to the licensee such that the licensee had standing to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the license terminated when the licensee shifted its business to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights and did not terminate when the licensee shifted its operations to enforcement. The court found the licensee could sue in its own name without joining the university. This clarifies the standard for when an exclusive license is tantamount to an assignment for standing purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer guidance that broad exclusive licenses conferring all substantial rights grant independent standing to sue, without needing to join the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on challenging the standing of exclusive licensees, and face continued exposure to enforcement actions by licensing entities that may not actively practice the patent.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of proprietary automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating the jury verdict. The decision affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret owners benefit from expanded latitude in presenting damages theories and from protection of jury verdicts on contract damages, strengthening enforcement of proprietary technology rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives after licensing third-party software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potential for significant damages awards at retrial.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results without specifying which method defines the claimed range.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of the '287 patent are invalid as indefinite because the specification identified multiple MVTR testing methods (upright, inverted, and Mocon) that produce different results, and skilled artisans could not determine with reasonable certainty which method defines the claimed MVTR range. This reinforces that functional performance limitations tied to variable test conditions can render claims indefinite.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials and textile industries can challenge patents with performance-based limitations where the specification fails to identify a single definitive testing protocol.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming functional performance ranges must ensure their specifications clearly specify a single testing methodology, or risk invalidation for indefiniteness.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages award and infringement finding were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to telecommunications technology patents, distinguishing between claims that recite specific technical implementations and those that may be directed to abstract mathematical optimization.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific, technically implemented improvements in communications standards retain strong protection, and the affirmance of damages and infringement findings supports enforcement of standard-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, though the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty for broadly claimed signal processing inventions.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching impedance to 'the characteristic impedance of the air' are invalid for lack of enablement, even if the claims are not indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds, finding that the patent did not enable the full scope of the claims as construed. The decision demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on grounds not relied upon below, and reinforces that claims whose scope extends beyond what the specification enables are invalid under § 112(a).
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to sustain invalidity findings on alternative grounds, providing additional avenues to challenge overly broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving indefiniteness challenges may still be invalidated for lack of enablement if the specification does not support the full claimed scope.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims directed to a float tool used in oil and gas well casing operations, and whether infringement and damages findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment of infringement and damages and remanded for further proceedings, finding error in the district court's claim construction of 'internal diameter' as used in the '445 patent claims directed to oil and gas wellbore tools. The case impacts the significant energy services patent litigation between NCS and Nine Energy over competing casing flotation devices.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the energy services sector benefit from more precise claim construction standards, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas equipment space face the burden of retrial following claim construction reversals, with potential narrowing of their patent scope on remand.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, finding the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed suit on electronic sweepstakes system claims despite multiple § 101 rejections of related applications by the PTO and a sister court's invalidation of closely related patent claims. The decision signals heightened scrutiny of patent assertions where there are strong indicators of ineligibility.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers who prevail on § 101 grounds have stronger prospects for recovering attorneys' fees when patent holders persist in asserting claims despite clear warning signs of ineligibility.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions for pursuing infringement claims when related applications have been rejected on eligibility grounds.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms, pharmaceutical formulations, and methods of treating cancer with cabozantinib (L)-malate satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of the Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description, upholding the validity of Exelixis's patents protecting Cabometyx® (cabozantinib) against generic entry by MSN Laboratories. The decision reinforces the strength of pharmaceutical polymorph and salt-form patents when adequately supported by the specification.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from strong validation of polymorph and salt-form patent claims, providing continued protection against generic competitors and supporting exclusivity periods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the validity of formulation and polymorph patents is upheld.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract dispute regarding the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning whether T-Mobile owed an additional payment under a patent settlement agreement conditioned on asserted claims 'surviving' an ex parte reexamination. The court found the dispute was fundamentally one of contract interpretation under state law, not a patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for settlement agreement disputes involving patent proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements gain clarity that disputes over contractual payment terms tied to PTO proceedings may be litigated in regional circuits under state contract law, potentially before more favorable forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties expecting Federal Circuit review of patent-related settlement disputes may face unexpected jurisdictional transfers, adding cost and uncertainty to dispute resolution.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on § 101 eligibility grounds after already determining that venue is improper under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent eligibility grounds, holding that the court did not err in reaching the merits of a § 101 challenge even after finding venue was improper. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was held ineligible. The ruling allows district courts to issue § 101 determinations alongside venue dismissals, potentially preventing re-filing in other venues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain a binding § 101 eligibility ruling even when venue is improper, potentially precluding the patent holder from re-filing the same claims in a different district.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face the risk that a venue challenge will be coupled with a substantive eligibility dismissal, eliminating the ability to re-file in a more favorable forum.
